extra.message: SQL injection in login — Authentication bypass (e.g. `' OR '1'='1`) or full extraction of the users table via boolean/UNION-based injection [verified: login() at libuser.py:12 formats raw request.form username/password into SQL with no parameterization or sanitization, enabling auth bypass/injection.]

SQL injection in password change — Arbitrary SQL execution, e.g. update/overwrite arbitrary users' passwords or corrupt the users table [verified: password_change() at libuser.py:53 interpolates g.session['username'] (from unsigned cookie) and user-supplied password directly into an UPDATE statement with no parameterization.]

Hardcoded Fernet key allows forging authenticated session cookies for any user — Full account takeover / authentication bypass for any username by forging a valid session cookie offline [verified: Fernet key is hardcoded in libsession.py:9, publicly visible in source, allowing anyone to encrypt an arbitrary 'username|country' token and forge a valid vulpy_session cookie for any user with no further verification in load().]

TOTP/MFA secrets logged via SQL trace callback — TOTP shared secrets written to logs, allowing an attacker with log access to generate valid OTP codes and bypass MFA entirely [verified: conn.set_trace_callback(print) at line 78 logs the expanded SQL for the parameterized UPDATE, including the raw TOTP secret bound as a parameter, to stdout/logs.]

SQL injection in user registration — Injection during registration allowing arbitrary SQL execution (e.g. break out of the INSERT to run additional statements or corrupt data) [verified: create() at libuser.py:25 uses %-formatting to build an INSERT from raw request.form username/password with no validation.]

Plaintext password storage — Compromise of db_users.sqlite (or a SQL injection dump) reveals every user's password in cleartext, enabling credential-stuffing attacks against other services [verified: Passwords are stored and compared as plaintext in SQL with no hashing anywhere in libuser.py, despite passlib being available in the project.]

Missing authentication on API post listing endpoint — Any unauthenticated caller can enumerate and read any user's private posts by username [verified: do_post_list at bad/mod_api.py:48-51 has no authentication, decorator, or session check before calling libposts.get_posts(username), so any unauthenticated request can enumerate any user's posts by username.]

Unauthenticated IDOR on posts API endpoint (bad variant) — Any anonymous attacker can read any user's posts by guessing/enumerating usernames [verified: do_post_list at bad/mod_api.py:49 calls libposts.get_posts(username) directly with no authentication or ownership check, unlike do_post_create which requires libapi.authenticate; any anonymous caller can enumerate any user's posts.]

Password change without current-password verification — Any request bearing (even a forged) session for a username can silently overwrite that account's password, enabling account takeover [verified: bad/mod_user.py do_chpasswd changes password for g.session['username'] with no check of the current/old password, and sessions are unsigned base64 cookies, so access control on this sensitive action is genuinely absent.]

Debug mode enabled with hardcoded weak SECRET_KEY — With debug=True, an unhandled exception exposes the Werkzeug interactive debugger (RCE via the debugger console if PIN is guessed/leaked); the weak known SECRET_KEY lets an attacker forge Flask session signatures [verified: debug=True in app.run enables Werkzeug interactive debugger and SECRET_KEY='aaaaaaa' is trivially guessable, both on the reachable startup path with no compensating control.]

Flask app run with debug=True — If reachable by an attacker (e.g., misconfigured deployment), an unhandled exception exposes the Werkzeug debugger, potentially leading to remote code execution; also leaks stack traces/source and internal paths. [verified: debug=True is set directly in the app.run call, exposing the Werkzeug debugger which allows RCE if an unhandled exception occurs and the PIN is bypassed.]

Unauthenticated IDOR on posts API endpoint — Any unauthenticated attacker can read any user's posts by iterating usernames. [verified: do_post_list has no authentication or authorization check before calling libposts.get_posts(username), unlike do_post_create which requires libapi.authenticate; any anonymous request can enumerate any username's posts.]

Missing rate limiting / lockout on login and OTP verification — Unlimited online brute-force of user passwords and 6-digit TOTP codes, enabling account takeover [verified: do_login() in good/mod_user.py calls libuser.login() and libmfa.mfa_validate() with no attempt counter, lockout, or delay anywhere in the request path, and the 'failures' column exists in schema but is never read/incremented, confirming brute-force protection is genuinely absent.]

Flask debug mode enabled in running app — Remote code execution on the host via the Werkzeug interactive debugger if triggered on an unhandled exception. [verified: app.run(debug=True, ...) at good/vulpy.py:53 enables the Werkzeug interactive debugger with no PIN disabling or other mitigation, and any unhandled exception in a request handler would expose it.]

Weak PRNG and insecure world-readable file-based API key storage — API keys are predictable (non-cryptographic PRNG) and stored in a shared, world-readable location (/tmp), allowing local attackers or key prediction to hijack another user's API access [verified: random.getrandbits uses Mersenne Twister, not a CSPRNG, and keys are stored as world-readable filenames in shared /tmp with no permission hardening — both genuinely present with no compensating control.]

Sensitive data (plaintext passwords) logged via SQL trace callback — Plaintext usernames and passwords for every login/change attempt are written to application logs, exposing credentials to anyone with log access [verified: set_trace_callback(print) is set on every connection in libuser.py, causing full SQL including plaintext passwords to be printed to logs on every login/create/chpasswd call.]

No rate limiting on login/API key/OTP endpoints — Attackers can brute-force passwords or 6-digit TOTP codes online with unlimited attempts (mfa_validate is also unprotected in mod_mfa.py:47) [verified: No rate-limiting middleware/decorator exists anywhere in the app on login, key creation, or MFA validation endpoints, allowing unlimited brute-force attempts against passwords and TOTP codes.]

Hardcoded, weak Flask SECRET_KEY — Attacker who knows/guesses the secret can forge any Flask-signed token (flash messages, CSRF tokens if enabled, itsdangerous-signed cookies), potentially enabling session/CSRF forgery. [verified: SECRET_KEY is hardcoded to a trivial value checked into source, allowing forgery of any itsdangerous-signed data derived from it.]

Sensitive query parameters (password hashes, salts) written to logs via SQL trace callback — Password hashes and salts land in application logs, aiding offline cracking if logs are exposed or retained insecurely [verified: set_trace_callback(print) is called before every SQL execution in login/user_create/password_set, printing fully-interpolated SQL including plaintext scrypt-derived password hash and salt hex to stdout on password set/login. No control suppresses this in the reachable request path.]

Sensitive query data logged via SQL trace callback in libposts — Usernames and query data written to stdout/logs, aiding credential/session harvesting from log files [verified: conn.set_trace_callback(print) at libposts.py:10 logs the fully expanded SQL including the bound username on every get_posts() call, an unconditional reachable sink.]

Sensitive post content logged via SQL trace callback — User-submitted content and usernames leak into logs [verified: conn.set_trace_callback(print) at libposts.py:24 logs the fully expanded INSERT including username and post text on every post() call, an unconditional reachable sink.]
